title: Budget, batching & residency review - Stonebridge Labs intake
summary: Intro discovery on per-token economics, tradeoffs between hosted/dedicated/private, and residency requirements. Customer has strict budget lanes and wants concrete levers (batching, KV cache, quantization) and a pilot scope that fits procurement timeline.
next_steps: Redwood to send a tailored cost model spreadsheet
SE to run a 24-hour throughput benchmark with their sample prompts
Schedule pilot kickoff for week of 6/8
action_items: Jordan Lee - Build benchmark runner + initial numbers - due 2026-05-28
Maya Patel - Send pricing and pilot contract template - due 2026-05-24
Aisha Rahman - Provide sample prompt set and traffic profile - due 2026-05-25
transcript:
[00:00:00] Maya (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. We're Maya from Redwood, joined by Jordan on the SE side and Clara. How's everyone doing?
[00:00:08] Aisha (Stonebridge - CTO): Good, thanks. Busy week but excited to get into this.
[00:00:12] Tomas (Head of ML): Hi all. We wanted to focus on the cost levers — per token and batching mostly — and how residency will impact price.
[00:00:21] Maya: Awesome. Quick agenda: 1) understand your workload and budget lanes, 2) go through hosted vs dedicated vs private tradeoffs, 3) actionable levers (batching, KV cache, quantization), 4) next steps. Sound okay?
[00:00:35] Erin (Finance): Yes, please. We have a hard cap for year 1 and need to see a credible runway.
[00:00:40] Jordan (SE): To ground the convo, can you share volume — rps or tokens per month — and latency needs?
[00:00:48] Aisha: Sure. Right now POC phase: roughly 6M tokens/month, bursty peaks up to 40 RPS. Latency SLO is 150-250ms p95 for the customer-facing flows, internal flows can tolerate 400-500.
[00:01:03] Tomas: Typical prompt length 220 tokens, responses avg 140 tokens. We're using a smaller open model today but want better quality without exploding cost.
[00:01:14] Maya: Great. So your key constraints are budget + a tight p95 for some routes. On residency — do you need on-prem or just VPC in a specific cloud region?
[00:01:25] Aisha: We need EU data residency for EU customers and a private VPC for the payment reconciliation service — not full on-prem yet but procurement may request it later.
[00:01:36] Erin: Also, everything touching PII has to be encrypted with our KMS and logged for audits.
[00:01:41] Jordan: Understood. Redwood's Private option supports on-prem or customer-managed VPC; we can plug in your KMS and we keep audit logs. Dedicated gives you isolated GPU pools without the overhead of installing. Hosted is fastest to start but has cross-region routing considerations.
[00:01:58] Tomas: Cost-wise, how big is the gap between hosted and dedicated? Ballpark numbers please.
[00:02:03] Maya: Ballpark: for steady medium models, hosted per-token is higher because it includes shared infra and managed ops — but it's simple. Dedicated is cheaper per-unit at scale because you commit capacity; you're paying reserved GPU costs but unit cost drops. Private has an additional platform fee and ops leg but can be cheapest if you amortize hardware and run at high utilization.
[00:02:21] Aisha: We're not sure we'll hit the utilization to justify dedicated in year 1. That's a worry.
[00:02:26] Jordan: That's common. That's where levers like batching and KV prefix caching buy you headroom — they reduce tokens sent to the model and effective cost. For example, if you can cache common prefixes or completions you could cut token spend by 20-40% depending on hit rate.
[00:02:41] Tomas: Can you show an example calculation?
[00:02:44] Jordan: Sure. If you have 6M input tokens + 3.6M output tokens per month (approx based on your averages), that's 9.6M tokens. If your hosted rate is X per 1K tokens — we'll put placeholders — at 0.6 per 1K it's ~ $5.8k/month. If caching reduces 30% of output tokens, that becomes ~ $4.1k. Batching reduces latency vs cost tradeoffs; with continuous batching you can increase utilization of GPUs and lower effective per-token kernel overhead.
[00:03:10] Erin: Wait sorry the 0.6 number — is that an actual Redwood hosted price or just an illustration?
[00:03:15] Maya: Illustration for discussion. I'll send exact pricing in the spreadsheet but want to ground the math now.
[00:03:20] Aisha: How about quantization — we heard Q8 and Q4ish options. Does quality degrade a lot?
[00:03:27] Jordan: We recommend a quantization profile per model. Some models tolerate 8-bit quantization well with minor quality impact; others need 4-bit or mixed precision. Quantization can reduce GPU memory and enable cheaper instance families. But you'd want evals on your prompts — Redwood Optimize suggests profiles per workload and flags regressions.
[00:03:44] Tomas: Could the quantization and batching combined push us to a cheaper config that still meets p95 250ms?
[00:03:50] Jordan: Possibly. For smaller sequence lengths (~360 tokens total) and with KV caching for common prefixes, we can keep latency low with optimized kernels, especially on A100 or better. If you need strict p95 for customer-facing flows, the pattern is often: keep that route on a lower-latency variant (dedicated or hosted with reserved capacity) and route internal/background traffic to cheaper variants.
[00:04:09] Erin: That routing sounds promising. Will routing increase complexity and cost?
[00:04:13] Maya: There is some policy complexity but Redwood Console supports per-route models and automatic failover. Cost-wise you pay for the active requests. The benefit is you only pay premium for the small percent of traffic needing low latency.
[00:04:24] [00:04:30] Tomas: On the residency question — if we need a VPC in eu-west-1 for production, does hosted support region isolation?
[00:04:36] Jordan: Hosted can pin requests to a region in many cases, but for strict residency + KMS we recommend Dedicated in that region or Redwood Private in your VPC. Hosted has global endpoints that can be region scoped but regulated customers prefer dedicated/private.
[00:04:51] Aisha: Procurement will ask for SOC2 docs and proof of key separation. Can you supply that?
[00:04:56] Maya: Yes, we'll share SOC2 and our KMS integration guide. We can also provide a diagram of key flow and audit log snapshots.
[00:05:04] Erin: Great.
[00:05:06] [00:05:12] Aisha: One thing — what about burst capacity? We have spikes to 40 RPS; if we pick Dedicated could we burst into hosted?
[00:05:19] Jordan: Yes, Redwood supports burst/overflow policies. You can configure fallback to hosted-compatible model variants when dedicated capacity exhausts. There's an associated fallback cost but it avoids throttling.
[00:05:30] Tomas: How transparent is billing for mixed-mode routing? We want per-route cost attribution.
[00:05:36] Maya: Console gives token-level attribution by model and route. We'll include an example in the cost spreadsheet so you can map to your internal chargeback.
[00:05:45] [00:06:00] Aisha: Okay, can we dig into a concrete pilot scope? We need something under a $20k run rate for the POC month.
[00:06:07] Erin: Year-one cap is $180k, but POC must be under $20k to fit procurement's quick-start.
[00:06:14] Jordan: For a POC under $20k, we typically recommend hosted to get going fast and instrument caching/batching. If after a month you see predictable throughput above X tokens/day we move to dedicated commit.
[00:06:24] Tomas: What's X in your playbook?
[00:06:26] Jordan: Depends on model and burst. For your averages, maybe ~50M tokens/month would justify dedicated at meaningful savings. That's well past your POC. So hosted POC + caching/batching seems reasonable.
[00:06:39] Erin: That aligns with procurement's appetite. But they want a firm estimate so they can approve the credit card.
[00:06:45] Maya: We'll produce a couple of scenarios in the spreadsheet: hosted-optimized with caching (expected cost), hosted without caching (worst case), and a projected dedicated breakeven run-rate.
[00:06:55] Tomas: Can you include quantization scenarios too — like Q8 vs Q4 runtime impacts?
[00:06:59] Jordan: Yes. We'll include quality tradeoff notes; we'll flag anything that causes >1% regression on your eval set.
[00:07:06] [00:07:20] Aisha: On security, we need to confirm logs retention and deletion for EU customers.
[00:07:25] Clara (Redwood): We can configure log retention policies per account and integrate with your SIEM; deletion requests and data export are supported via the console and API.
[00:07:33] Erin: Perfect.
[00:07:35] Tomas: A question on the KV cache — how easy is it to integrate? Do we need code changes?
[00:07:40] Jordan: Typically minimal. For prefix caching, it's often a small wrapper in the calling service: check cache -> if miss call Redwood. Redwood also has built-in prefix caching policies if you host the model on Dedicated/Private. For hosted, you'll implement caching client-side or use our edge cache offering for some patterns.
[00:07:57] Aisha: If we implement client-side caching, we risk staleness for dynamic prompts.
[00:08:02] Jordan: Right, that's a tradeoff. Cache TTL and invalidation strategies are part of the design. For high-fidelity customer-facing flows you may prefer short TTLs or rely on KV cache for non-personalized pieces.
[00:08:12] [00:08:30] Erin: Let's talk procurement bar — they will ask for terms on incident SLA and uptime. What SLAs do you provide for Dedicated vs Hosted?
[00:08:38] Maya: Dedicated comes with SLA-backed uptime and latency targets in the contract. Hosted has operational SLAs for throughput and availability for paid tiers; Private can be contractually negotiated with enterprise support. We'll surface the exact SLA language in the contract attachment.
[00:08:53] Tomas: Are there termination fees for reserved capacity?
[00:08:56] Maya: There are commitment terms with discounts for annual reserved capacity. We can propose a pilot-friendly monthly commit with a small cancellation window if that helps.
[00:09:06] Aisha: That might help procurement.
[00:09:09] [00:09:20] Tomas: Any hidden overheads around model version pinning or rollbacks? We need reproducibility for compliance.
[00:09:26] Jordan: Redwood supports model pinning, versioned rollouts, and lineage metadata. Rollbacks are straightforward and we provide invocation logs to trace inputs/outputs (with redaction if required).
[00:09:36] Aisha: Good.
[00:09:39] [00:09:55] Erin: Back to cost — can you give an example of how batching latency vs cost behaves? Say if we allow 50ms additional latency, how much can we expect to save?
[00:10:02] Jordan: Rough estimates: batching is workload-dependent. For small requests, increasing batching window to 50-100ms can aggregate requests and reduce per-request overhead by 10-30%. For heavy token-gen requests the benefit is lower. We can quantify for your real traffic with a 24–48 hour benchmark.
[00:10:16] Tomas: Let's do that benchmark. We'll provide a representative trace.
[00:10:19] Maya: Great — Jordan will run it.
[00:10:22] [00:10:30] Aisha: A couple more nitty-gritty items: 1) can we restrict model catalog choices in production? 2) is there an approval workflow?
[00:10:38] Jordan: Yes on both. You can restrict which models are allowed per route and require approvals for rollouts. We support RBAC and SSO to gate changes.
[00:10:46] Erin: On SSO — we use SAML and Okta.
[00:10:49] Clara: We support SAML/OAuth and can provide SSO onboarding docs.
[00:10:53] [00:11:05] Tomas: One risk we see is stealth cost when experiments start and cached hit rates fall. How do we monitor regressions?
[00:11:12] Maya: Redwood Console has quality and cost monitoring tied to prompt sets — you can flag an eval set and watch regressions and unit economics. Alerts can be set for token burn or cost anomalies.
[00:11:23] Erin: Okay that gives finance comfort.
[00:11:27] [00:11:45] Aisha: Let's summarize next steps.
[00:11:48] Maya: We'll send: 1) tailored cost model spreadsheet with hosted + caching scenarios and a dedicated breakeven, 2) SOC2 and KMS integration docs, 3) an SE-run benchmark using your prompt set, 4) a pilot contract template and suggested timeboxed commit.
[00:12:03] Erin: Do you have a turnaround on the spreadsheet? We need it by Monday for procurement.
[00:12:07] Maya: We'll get it to you by 2026-05-24 COB.
[00:12:11] Tomas: And the benchmark?
[00:12:13] Jordan: I'll run it after we get the prompt set; target results by 2026-05-28.
[00:12:18] Aisha: Sounds good. Anything else?
[00:12:22] [00:12:35] Erin: Procurement might ask about shared model artifacts — do you persist inputs/outputs?
[00:12:40] Clara: By default we store logs for a configurable retention; we can anonymize or disable storage. For Private you control persistence.
[00:12:49] Tomas: One last thing on routing: if we route internal traffic to cheaper variants, how do we test for quality drift?
[00:12:55] Jordan: Use shadow/traffic mirroring and evals. Redwood supports mirrored requests to a second model for offline evaluation before switching routes.
[00:13:05] Aisha: Ok that addresses many concerns. We'll share the prompt set and traffic profile by EOD tomorrow.
[00:13:12] Maya: Thanks — we'll follow up with the materials and set the pilot kickoff once procurement signs off.
[00:13:18] [00:13:30] Erin: Thanks everyone.
[00:13:32] [end of recorded transcript — meeting lasted 54 minutes total, remainder of time included silent onboarding and a quick hallway chat about holiday schedules which the recorder picked up].

Notes about transcript quality: occasional mis-heard words (e.g., "K-V cash" for KV cache) and slight speaker attribution shifts. We preserved disfluencies and typical sales cadence.
